title: Sheridan Lake Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Sheridan Lake wells have a 78-foot median depth; finished well costs are modeled at $8,700-$16,300.
intro_html:
Buying land near Sheridan Lake means looking closely at the well record, not just the presence of a permit. Records within 12 miles show 260 permitted wells, including 112 recorded as constructed. Of those, 151 report total depth, 55 report pump yield, and 11 report static water level.

This is plains country, with wells completed in unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, the Ogallala, and the Dakota. The local records include domestic, stock, and irrigation wells, so the reported yield and construction details can vary substantially from one parcel to the next. Use this page to set expectations, then have a driller and water professional review the specific property.

sections.heading: Sheridan Lake well depth: usually shallow, sometimes not
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Sheridan Lake is 78 feet. The middle half runs from 46 to 138 feet, meaning a typical drilling bid may be based on a relatively shallow hole, but neighboring wells can differ. The 90th percentile is 210 feet, and the deepest recorded well reaches 1,590 feet.

Depths are concentrated below 100 feet, accounting for 68% of the depth records. Another 26% fall between 100 and 300 feet, while 3% are between 300 and 600 feet and 3% exceed 600 feet. The local mix includes alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, along with permits naming fractured-bedrock aquifers. A driller should check nearby logs rather than price your well from the median alone.

sections.heading: What Sheridan Lake wells produce
sections.html:
Reported pump yields are generally favorable, but the data set is limited to 55 wells. The median reported yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half spans 12.0 to 124.0 gallons per minute. That wide range is a reminder that production can change sharply between locations.

Seventy-one percent of reported wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute. Twenty percent fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 9% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute. A buyer should still ask for the well completion report, pumping information, and any storage-tank plan. A permit does not guarantee that a new hole will match the strongest nearby well.

sections.heading: Water levels around Sheridan Lake
sections.html:
Only 11 wells in the records report a static water level, so this is a thin sample rather than a complete groundwater survey. The median depth to static water is 86 feet. The middle half ranges from 46 to 412 feet, showing that water levels can differ substantially across the area.

The permit history does not provide enough static-water observations to call a reliable decade-by-decade rise or decline. Treat the reported 86-foot median as a planning reference, not a guaranteed pumping level for your lot. Before buying or building, have a contractor review nearby well logs and measure the existing well after it has rested. Pump setting, casing, storage, and electrical design should follow the actual well rather than a countywide assumption.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Sheridan Lake, and when
sections.html:
The records include permits from the 1950s through the 2020s, with the newest permit year listed as 2025. Permit activity was highest in the 1970s and 1990s, with 42 permits in each decade. There were 20 in the 1960s, 10 in the 1980s, 21 in the 2000s, 16 in the 2010s, and 3 in the 2020s. These counts describe permits, not necessarily currently working wells.

Kemp'S Well Service (Kemp, George) appears most often, with 38 records. Hoffman (Hoffman, Earl) appears on 11, and Weishaar Drilling & Supply Inc (Stanton, Floyd) on 8. Those records can help identify local drilling history, but confirm current licensing, availability, scope, and references before selecting a contractor. Colorado DWR permit and construction records remain the starting point.

sections.heading: Sheridan Lake well drilling cost
sections.html:
For the local alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the cost model uses a drilling rate of $35 to $55 per foot. At the 78-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $2,700 to $4,300. That is only the hole, not a complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $8,700 to $16,300 at the median depth. A deeper-than-typical hole, difficult access, casing or grout requirements, electrical distance, and water-storage needs can move the bid higher. Ask for a written estimate that separates drilling, casing, grout, development, pump equipment, trenching, electrical work, testing, and permit-related work. The 1,590-foot record shows why a depth allowance matters on an unusual site.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying a Sheridan Lake lot
sections.html:
Five PFAS sampling or contamination sites are mapped within about 10 miles. There are no historic mine features and no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in the mapped facts, but that does not replace a property-specific water test. Test an existing well for bacteria, nitrate, and other concerns recommended by a qualified laboratory; ask whether the well has a treatment history and review the chain of custody.

Low yield is not represented in the reported records below 1 gallon per minute, but only 55 wells report yield and a dry hole remains a construction risk. Confirm well location, access for a rig, setbacks from septic components, and the intended household use. Colorado DWR permits govern the well, and an exempt household-use well has a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit. Irrigation or expanded use may require different water-rights planning.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Sheridan Lake, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Sheridan Lake is 78 feet, with the middle half from 46 to 138 feet. Sixty-eight percent are under 100 feet. Depths vary, though: the 90th percentile is 210 feet and the deepest record is 1,590 feet. Have a driller review nearby logs before accepting a fixed-depth estimate.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Sheridan Lake?
faq.a: The local model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 78-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $2,700 to $4,300. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $8,700 to $16,300. Actual bids depend on depth, access, casing, grout, equipment, and site conditions.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Sheridan Lake?
faq.a: Among 55 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 12.0 to 124.0 gallons per minute. Seventy-one percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 9% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute. These figures are useful for screening, not a guarantee for a new well.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Sheridan Lake, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a permit or yield record. Five PFAS sampling or contamination sites are mapped within about 10 miles, so test an existing well through a qualified laboratory. Review bacteria, nitrate, and other locally appropriate tests, along with any treatment history. A new well should also be tested after construction and before regular household use.

faq.q: What should I check before buying land with a well near Sheridan Lake?
faq.a: Review the Colorado DWR permit, construction report, measured water level, pump information, and recent water tests. Nearby records show a 78-foot median depth and 15.0-gallon-per-minute median reported yield, but only 11 wells report static water level and 55 report yield. Confirm septic setbacks, rig access, electrical needs, intended use, and any required water-rights planning.
